implementation_notes: The idiom's home: std::remove/remove_if partitions the range so that the retained elements are in [first, result) in their original order and returns result, and the container's range erase then destroys the tail - v.erase(std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), pred), v.end()). The sequence type supplies the erase, which is why the two calls are inseparable: the algorithm sees only an iterator pair and cannot change the container's size, exactly as the Wikibooks motivation puts it. C++11 is the practical floor because the compaction is specified in terms of move assignment from then on, so move-only element types work. Keep the explicit form when the tail must be inspected before it is erased, when the survivor range is needed (for example to hand it to another call first), or when the toolchain predates C++20; on associative containers it does not apply at all - use the container's own erase or, since C++20, std::erase_if.
pitfalls: Calling std::remove without the erase step: nothing is removed, the size is unchanged, and the tail holds moved-from elements that still satisfy nothing you meant to keep.
v.erase(it) with a single argument fed by the algorithm's return value compiles but erases exactly one element - always pass v.end() as the second argument.

Wrong container: on std::map/std::set/std::unordered_* and on std::list these algorithm overloads are the wrong tool (use erase(key), the member remove_if, or C++20 std::erase_if), because those containers erase per node instead of compacting.

variants.name: C++20 std::erase / std::erase_if free functions
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 adds free functions that expand to exactly the classic two steps (auto it = std::remove_if(c.begin(), c.end(), pred); auto r = c.end() - it; c.erase(it, c.end()); return r;) in one call, which also returns the number of erased elements. They exist for every standard sequence and string container and - unlike the two-step - for associative containers (std::map, std::set, std::unordered_*), where erasing by predicate cannot be expressed with std::remove_if at all. Prefer them whenever the toolchain is C++20: the intent is stated once, the mechanism belongs to the library, and the count comes back. The explicit form remains necessary only for user-defined containers that provide no overload, or for code that must still build as C++17.
pitfalls: Requires C++20 headers and the ADL-visible overload; on a user-defined container the call does not compile (it is not a member), so pre-C++20 targets still need the explicit two-step or a wrapper.

std::erase(c, value) and std::erase_if(c, pred) are different overloads: passing a predicate to std::erase tries to compare elements against it, which either fails to compile or, with a transparent element type, compares against something unexpected.
